chapters.title: Chapter 3: What Sits on Top of the Slabs

lessons.title: The Tax Rebate: Why Income Up to 12 Lakh Can Mean Zero Tax

body.text: The 4 lakh nil band is not the real zero-tax limit. The rebate is. For a resident individual under the new regime, it cancels up to ₹60,000 of slab tax, which is exactly the slab tax on ₹12 lakh.

children.text: In Chapter 2 you computed slab tax on dozens of incomes. For a huge share of Indian taxpayers, that slab tax is never actually paid. A school teacher in Lucknow with ₹11 lakh of taxable income has ₹50,000 of slab tax on paper and pays zero. The reason is the rebate, the first adjustment applied after the slab calculation.

body.label: Where the Rebate Lives
body.context: Most taxpayers and payroll teams still call it "the 87A rebate", so expect to hear both names for years.

children.text: The Rule in One Line

cells: Slab tax or ₹60,000, whichever is lower
Slab tax or ₹12,500, whichever is lower

body.caption: For resident individuals under the new regime. Marginal relief for incomes slightly above ₹12 lakh is a separate adjustment

children.text: The numbers are designed to fit together. New regime slab tax on exactly ₹12,00,000 is ₹60,000, and the maximum rebate is ₹60,000. Old regime slab tax on exactly ₹5,00,000 for someone below 60 is ₹12,500, and the maximum rebate is ₹12,500. In each regime, the rebate is sized to cancel slab tax completely right up to the income limit.
Where the Rebate Sits in the Calculation
Compute Total Income (Chapter 1).
Apply the slabs, and any special rates, to get tax on Total Income (Chapter 2).
Subtract the rebate, and marginal relief if applicable.
This lesson and the next.
Add surcharge, for incomes above ₹50 lakh.
Add 4% health and education cess on the result.

body.text: Because cess is calculated on tax after the rebate, a full rebate also wipes out the cess. Four percent of zero is zero. That is why a resident with ₹12 lakh of Total Income pays genuinely nothing, not a small cess amount.

body.title: Why not just make the first ₹12 lakh a nil slab?

children.text: A nil slab up to ₹12 lakh would give every taxpayer the ₹60,000 benefit, including someone earning ₹2 crore. A rebate gives the full ₹60,000 only to residents with Total Income up to ₹12 lakh, and nothing to those above it (apart from the narrow marginal relief band). The government gets to offer zero tax to the middle class at a fraction of the revenue cost. The price of that targeting is a sharp edge at the limit, which is exactly what the next lesson deals with.
Three Traps That Deny the Rebate
Trap 1: you are not a resident individual.
Non-residents, HUFs, AOPs and firms get no rebate at any income. An NRI with ₹6 lakh of rent from a flat in Pune pays full slab tax of ₹10,000 plus cess.
Trap 2: the ₹12 lakh test uses Total Income, including special-rate income.

Capital gains count towards the ₹12 lakh limit even though they are taxed at their own rates. Salary of ₹11 lakh plus ₹2 lakh of short-term gains on shares takes Total Income to ₹13 lakh, and the rebate on the salary is lost.
Trap 3: under the new regime, the rebate cannot be used against tax on special-rate income.

Even when Total Income is within ₹12 lakh, the rebate cancels only tax on slab-rate income. Tax on short-term gains on listed shares, long-term gains above the exemption and similar special-rate income must still be paid.

Take Tanvi, a marketing executive in Indore. Her Total Income is ₹11,00,000: ₹10,00,000 of salary after the standard deduction, plus ₹1,00,000 of short-term gains from selling shares she bought through Zerodha less than 12 months earlier. Slab tax on the ₹10 lakh is ₹40,000, and the rebate cancels it. Short-term gains on listed shares are taxed at a special rate of 20%, so she owes ₹20,000 on the gains, which the rebate cannot touch. With cess she pays ₹20,800. Chapter 4 explains how special-rate income works.

body.text: Trap 3 was the subject of real disputes over earlier years, when the ITR utility stopped allowing the rebate against special-rate income and taxpayers challenged it. The law has since been amended to state explicitly that, under the new regime, the rebate is not available on tax on special-rate income. If you have capital gains and income near ₹12 lakh, do not assume your tax is zero.

body.title: The old regime cliff at ₹5 lakh

children.text: Suresh, 40, is on the old regime. At Total Income of ₹4,90,000 his slab tax is ₹12,000 and the rebate cancels it: tax payable ₹0. If his Total Income is ₹5,10,000 instead, slab tax is ₹12,500 + 20% of ₹10,000 = ₹14,500, there is no rebate and no marginal relief, and with cess he pays ₹15,080. An extra ₹20,000 of income costs him ₹15,080 of tax. Old regime taxpayers just above ₹5 lakh often find that one more eligible deduction, such as a top-up to an ELSS or PPF investment within the old regime's limits, pays for itself many times over.

children.text: Practice

body.title: How Much Rebate?
body.prompt: Meghna, a resident nurse at a Kochi hospital, is on the new regime with Total Income of ₹9,50,000, all from salary. What rebate does she get?
body.explanation: Slab tax is ₹20,000 + 10% of ₹1,50,000 = ₹35,000. Her Total Income is within ₹12 lakh, so the rebate is the lower of ₹35,000 and ₹60,000, which is ₹35,000. Her tax payable is zero.

body.title: Who Gets the Rebate?
body.question: Each of these taxpayers is on the new regime with Total Income of ₹10,00,000 of slab-rate income. Who can claim the rebate?
options: The Sharma family HUF in Jaipur, earning rent from inherited shops
Arvind, an Indian citizen living in Dubai who is a non-resident for the year
Rekha, a resident salaried employee in Nagpur
A two-partner design firm in Chandigarh
body.explanation: The rebate is only for resident individuals. An HUF is not an individual, Arvind is not a resident, and a firm pays a flat rate with no rebate at all. Rekha's ₹40,000 of slab tax is fully cancelled.

body.title: Rebate vs Deduction
body.textWithBlank: A deduction reduces your income, while a rebate reduces your ___ directly.
body.explanation: A deduction saves tax only at your marginal rate. A rebate removes tax rupee for rupee, which is why a ₹60,000 rebate is worth exactly ₹60,000 to someone who qualifies.

body.title: The Highest Zero-Tax Salary
body.scenario: Aniket, a resident software developer in Pune, is on the new regime. His basic salary is ₹6,00,000 and his only income is salary. HR is willing to route part of his CTC into an employer NPS contribution of up to 14% of basic.
body.prompt: What is the highest gross salary, including the employer NPS contribution, at which Aniket still pays zero income tax? Show the working.
body.modelAnswer: The employer NPS deduction can be up to 14% of ₹6,00,000, which is ₹84,000. Working backwards from the ₹12,00,000 Total Income limit: add back the ₹84,000 NPS deduction and the ₹75,000 standard deduction. Gross salary of ₹13,59,000 gives Total Income of ₹13,59,000 − ₹75,000 − ₹84,000 = ₹12,00,000. Slab tax is ₹60,000, the rebate cancels all of it, and he pays zero. Above ₹13,59,000 the rebate is lost, apart from marginal relief. The trade-off is that ₹84,000 a year is locked into NPS until retirement.

points: The rebate under section 156 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (section 87A of the 1961 Act) is subtracted from tax after the slabs are applied
New regime: up to ₹60,000 for resident individuals with Total Income up to ₹12 lakh. Old regime: up to ₹12,500 up to ₹5 lakh
With the ₹75,000 standard deduction, a resident's salary of up to ₹12,75,000 attracts zero tax under the new regime
Cess is charged after the rebate, so a full rebate means genuinely zero tax
Non-residents, HUFs and firms get no rebate
Special-rate income counts towards the ₹12 lakh limit, and under the new regime the rebate cannot be used against tax on it
A rebate reduces tax rupee for rupee; a deduction or exemption only saves tax at your marginal rate

body.text: Rebate limits shown are for resident individuals for tax year 2026-27. Historical figures in the timeline are summarised for context. Limits can change in any Union Budget. This lesson is for education only and is not tax advice.
